quote: Now, Kevin, one thing I'm a little concerned about is you've got some trees that are putting some shade on the home.
stewart_read: This is the root of the whole disputed trajectory: the rep raises the shade concern unprompted and early, before any cost pushback has occurred, which supports the reading that it started as a genuine qualifying question rather than a manufactured exit. Its later use as an instant hard DQ right after the cost objection is what turns this from legitimate qualification into a questionable pattern.
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive read: the rep spotted the shade issue on Google Maps ahead of time and was always going to raise it regardless of how the cost conversation went, meaning the timing with the objection is coincidental rather than opportunistic.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to quantify shade impact (which side of the roof, single tree vs full canopy) before treating it as a DQ trigger — right now the concern is raised, dropped mid-sentence when the customer objects, then resurrected as a full disqualifier without new information.

quote: My my I'm not cutting my trees down. My average bill, quite frankly
stewart_read: Customer states his actual bill is low and defends the tree in the same breath — this maps to the schema's objection_inversion trigger (cost objection) but the rep never inverts it; instead the rep later validates the low bill as if that settles the matter.
coaching_implication: A flip here ('at $76-81/month you may not be the target customer, but let's see what the numbers show anyway') keeps the door open without over-promising; validating the objection outright as the rep does forecloses the conversation.

quote: the highest bill I've ever had was a $109. And my average bill, I'd say, over a course of twelve months is around 76 to $81.
stewart_read: Customer hands the rep a precise bill figure and even quotes a specific payback-period claim ('breakeven over twenty one years... used to be a thirty six year payback'), both usable anchors. The rep never reflects the number back or challenges the stale payback figure with anything current.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to engage the payback-period claim directly ('that's actually changed — let me show you what it looks like now') instead of letting it stand unchallenged before disqualifying.

quote: Yeah. I mean, I I totally see where you're coming from. You're right. Your bill isn't extremely high.
stewart_read: Rather than reframing the low bill as still worth reviewing (e.g., against future rate increases or usage growth), the rep fully concedes the objection, which removes any basis for continuing the conversation and sets up the DQ that follows two lines later.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic read: if the rep genuinely believed the home was unworkable due to shade, conceding the bill point costs nothing since the call was ending anyway. But the concession comes before the shade rationale is fully stated, so it reads as capitulation to the cost objection first.
coaching_implication: Replay this line with the rep — validating an objection outright, without any redirect, is the moment the call becomes unrecoverable regardless of the shade issue.

quote: yeah, like you said, you're not open to removing the trees at all, so solar won't work for you. I can just remove you from my list.
stewart_read: The rep declares the home categorically unworkable based on one tree's shade without citing any specific technical threshold (panel placement, percentage shading, alternate roof faces). Ion's schema does not currently define shade/tree disqualification criteria with the same specificity it gives the credit qualifier — this is a genuine schema gap, not just a rep skill gap.
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive read: the rep may have real training on shade thresholds not reflected in this transcript, and the DQ is procedurally correct even if terse.
coaching_implication: Flag to Kenny: the schema has no populated shade/tree disqualification rule (only qualifiers.credit_qualifier and dq_rules cover other hard gates). Until that's defined, reps are free-forming a DQ call with no stated standard, which is coachable both for this rep and for schema-building.

quote: How would you move a 250 year old tree?
stewart_read: Customer's pushback signals he does not fully accept the DQ rationale — he's questioning the practicality of the rep's suggested fix, not agreeing solar is impossible. The rep does not explore whether panel placement or partial-shade design could still work around a single back tree.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic read: the rep may have already mentally qualified this as a dead lead given the low bill and firm no-cut stance, making further exploration low-value. But the customer explicitly says 'I'm more willing to listen' at 01:53, which the rep never revisits.
coaching_implication: Note the missed signal at 01:53 ('I'm more willing to listen') — customer left a door open that the rep did not walk back through before ending the call.

quote: I'll put that here. If things change, you know, if you ever wanna look at options, feel free to give me a call. I'm happy to help.
stewart_read: The call ends with no next step owned by the rep, no bill document collected, and no specific follow-up date — a passive close entirely dependent on the customer calling back. Ion's schema's button_up protocol is written for booked appointments and does not define a DQ-exit standard, so this is also a schema gap worth flagging alongside the coaching note.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic read: if the home is genuinely disqualified by shade, a passive 'call me if things change' is an appropriate low-effort close since there is nothing to book. But the DQ itself is contested above, which undercuts this justification.
coaching_implication: If reps are going to soft-exit DQ calls, the floor needs a defined DQ-exit standard (e.g., offer to still send a no-obligation design, or note the file for review once trees are trimmed) rather than leaving it to individual rep instinct.
